title: My Calendar I
description:
# My Calendar I

You are implementing a calendar. A new event may be booked only when it does not create a **double booking** with any event that was already accepted.

A **double booking** happens when two events have a non-empty intersection. Each event is represented by a half-open interval `[start, end)`, meaning every time `x` with `start <= x < end`. Two events that only touch at an endpoint, such as `[10, 20)` and `[20, 30)`, do not overlap.

Implement the `MyCalendar` class:

*   `MyCalendar()` initializes an empty calendar.
*   `boolean book(int start, int end)` returns `true` and stores the event if it can be added without a double booking. Otherwise it returns `false` and must leave the calendar unchanged.

In operation examples, the first array lists operations and the second lists their argument lists, paired by index and executed left to right. The first operation constructs the object; later operations use that same object. Outputs align by index too: constructors and void methods produce `null`; an empty argument list `[]` means no arguments.

## Example 1:

**Input**
["MyCalendar", "book", "book", "book"]
[[], [10, 20], [15, 25], [20, 30]]
**Output**
[null, true, false, true]
**Explanation**
`[10, 20)` is accepted. `[15, 25)` is rejected because it intersects `[10, 20)` on `[15, 20)`. `[20, 30)` is accepted because it only touches the first booking at time `20`, and the first booking does not include `20`.

## Constraints:

*   `0 <= start < end <= 10^9`
*   At most `1000` calls will be made to `book`.

solutions.name: TreeMap Neighbor Check
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store accepted intervals in a `TreeMap` from start time to end time. For a new interval, the only accepted events that can overlap it are the interval with the greatest start not larger than `start`, and the interval with the smallest start not smaller than `start`. Check those two neighbors before inserting.

## Key Insight

Once intervals are sorted by start time and the calendar never contains overlaps, a non-neighbor cannot jump across a valid neighbor to overlap the new interval. The half-open rule means `previousEnd == start` and `nextStart == end` are both safe.

## Complexity Analysis

Each neighbor lookup and insertion costs O(log n), where `n` is the number of accepted bookings. The calendar stores O(n) intervals.

solutions.name: Brute Force Interval List
solutions.description:
## Approach

Keep every accepted event in an unsorted list. To book `[start, end)`, scan all existing intervals and reject as soon as one satisfies `start < existingEnd && existingStart < end`. If no interval overlaps, append the new event.

## Key Insight

The overlap predicate is the most important baseline for this problem. For half-open intervals, two ranges overlap exactly when each starts before the other ends; equality at an endpoint is not an overlap.

## Complexity Analysis

A booking scans up to O(n) accepted events, and insertion is O(1). The list uses O(n) space.

solutions.name: Sorted Arrays with Binary Search
solutions.description:
## Approach

Maintain two parallel `ArrayList`s: sorted start times and their matching end times. Binary search finds the insertion index for the new start. Then check only the previous and next stored intervals; if both are compatible, insert the new start and end at that index.

## Key Insight

This is the array version of the ordered-neighbor idea. Binary search finds the only two possible conflicts, while the cost of keeping arrays sorted is paid during insertion.

## Complexity Analysis

Binary search is O(log n), but inserting into the middle of an array list shifts O(n) values, so each successful booking is O(n). Space is O(n).

solutions.name: Sweep-Line Delta with Rollback
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store sweep-line deltas in a `TreeMap`: add `+1` at each accepted start and `-1` at each accepted end. For a tentative booking, apply its two deltas, scan the prefix sum in time order, and reject if the active count ever becomes greater than one. On rejection, undo the two tentative deltas.

## Key Insight

This route directly models the definition of double booking. The rollback step is essential: a failed `book` call must leave the data structure exactly as it was before the attempt.

## Complexity Analysis

Each attempt scans O(n) distinct endpoints after O(log n) delta updates. The map stores O(n) endpoints.

solutions.name: Dynamic Segment Tree Occupancy
solutions.description:
## Approach

Build a dynamic segment tree over the coordinate range `[0, 10^9]`. Query the maximum occupancy on `[start, end - 1]`; if it is already positive, the new event overlaps an accepted booking. Otherwise add one to that range. Nodes are created only along touched paths.

## Key Insight

The time domain is huge, but each booking touches only O(log U) segment-tree nodes. This route is heavier than ordered-neighbor checks for Calendar I, yet it prepares the same range-counting machinery used by harder calendar variants.

## Complexity Analysis

Each query and update costs O(log U), where `U = 10^9 + 1`. A successful booking can allocate O(log U) nodes, so space is O(n log U) in the worst case.
